utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Andres Vatter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, my legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as everyone else present in this courtroom, including the interpreters. We have a witness today, but before we call the witness into the courtroom, I would like to provide you with the following information. The legal officer forwarded to the Prosecution on the 28th of -- 24th of May a list of documents which are either missing or incomplete or are illegible or are documents for which we have no translations, or documents in which translation issues have appeared. The Prosecution has informed us of the procedure they would follow following what the Trial Chamber said. They will do so by contacting the Chamber's legal officer. As far as these documents are concerned, I would like to say the following: With regard to Articles 12 and 14 of the Statute, the President of the Chamber guides the work of the Chamber. This work includes naturally all technical issues which might arise, and in particular issues that concern documents when they are presented, documents that might be tendered as evidence. As you know, 90(F) -- Rule 90(F) provides that the Trial Chamber can control the way in which the evidence is presented in order to ensure that the presentation of the evidence is efficient. As the parties are well aware, the Prosecution under Rule 66 must provide the Defence with the documents attached to the confirmed indictment. The Defence -- when the Defence requests this, the Prosecution must enable them to consult books and documents, as well as photographs, and items that they have in possession. And further to Rule 68 of the Rules, the Prosecution must provide the Defence with all information that might be exculpatory evidence. The Rules also provide - namely, Rule 68(B) - that the Prosecution should provide the Defence in an electronic form with a total -- with the totality of the documents that they have in their possession. As a result, all the documents that the Prosecution has can under certain conditions be provided to the Defence. That's the spirit and the text itself of the Rule. Last Friday, on the basis of this provision I personally stated that it was irritating that the article concerning the audiotape was not provided. In order to ensure that there is no misunderstanding concerning this term, the Petit Robert, the French dictionary, says the following about the term "facheux" or "irritating". It gives rise to certain inconveniences or is prejudicial. The Collins-Robert dictionary says the following about the term facheux. It says it is irritating. I raise this issue with regard to an answer provided by a witness. A witness said that he drafted an article on the basis of this audiotape. The Defence provided another article dated the 27th of June, 1993, DH181 is the number of the exhibit. But the article provided by the Defence wasn't the article that was produced after this audiotape. The Trial Chamber and naturally its President can under Rule 98 order that additional evidence be presented. At this point in time, the Trial Chamber has not deliberated to determine whether this press article should at a subsequent date be presented pursuant to Rule 98. I wanted to provide you with this information which I think should be useful for everyone. We have a witness scheduled for today, Mr. Mundis. Could you inform us of whether the witness is available for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness Dieter Schellschmidt is in fact available, and his evidence will be led by my colleague, Ms. Benjamin, this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. Are you receiving the interpretation into a language that you can understand, either French or English? If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. You will have to take the solemn declaration, but before you do so, I have to ask you your name. Could you first tell me your first and last names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dieter Schellschmidt. I am born on the 20th of May, 1935 in Forst, Brandenburg, Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume your nationality is German.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my nationality is German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a retired army officer. My last rank was lieutenant colonel. And I'm now acting as a manager of a non-governmental organisation in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what position did you hold and what duties did you perform in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a member of the ECMM, the European Community Monitoring Mission, on a six-month contract from February to end of August in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now ask the usher to show you the solemn declaration that I would like you to read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, you've been called here to testify about the events that took place in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and also about what happened at the beginning of 1994. You will first have to answer questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution, who are to your right. You have already had the opportunity of meeting them. After they have completed their examination-in-chief, you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Defence; they are to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. left. This stage is what we call the cross-examination. The purpose of the questions put to you by the Defence is to check the credibility of what you say and also to obtain any necessary information, any information that is relevant to the context within which these events took place. Once this stage has been completed, the Prosecution may take the floor again to conduct their re-examination. And once these three stages have been completed, the three Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions. Each Judge may ask you questions. We will listen to your answers, and the purpose of our questions is to obtain additional information or to clarify some of the answers you have provided to the parties, or if a Judge thinks that there is a matters that obscure, in such a case the Judge may also ask you a question. Once the Judges have asked your their questions and once you have answered their questions, the Defence has the right to ask you further questions, as well as the Prosecution. So roughly speaking, this is the procedure that will be followed here. To the extent that it is possible, try to provide complete and concise answers to the questions. It's true that these events took place over ten years ago, and if your memory is deficient, be frank and tell us that that is the case. The procedure that we follow here is on the whole an oral procedure, and sometimes it is supported by written evidence, so you might also be shown documents, but this is for the parties to decide, and this is why your answers are so important. If you encounter any difficulties, do let us know, and if you don't understand a question or if a question seems too complicated to you, ask the person putting the question to rephrase it in simple terms. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution. I don't know who will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Perhaps Ms. Benjamin. So if it is Ms. Benjamin who will be conducting the examination-in-chief, she may now take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, you have already indicated to the Trial Chamber your rank, but I would like you now to please briefly describe for the Trial Chamber your career and your experience and qualifications, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Actually, I joined the German Armed Forces in April 1957 as an officer candidate. My arm at this time was artillery. I was commissioned in 1959. At that time, I had already changed branches from artillery to maintenance corps. My first position was a platoon commander in that corps. In 1961, I signed up for a course at the academy of machinery of the German Armed Forces in Darmstadt, was accepted, and studied there for four years. I graduated in 1965 as a mechanical engineer. After that, I continued my education for one year in the United States at the US Army missile and ammunition school and returned to Germany in mid-July 1966, taking up a position again as platoon leader. Later on I became company commander, deputy commander of a maintenance battalion, and finally ended the -- my field career as a battalion commander. I was promoted lieutenant colonel in 1976. The same year, I was transferred to the general army officer in Koln, where I took several positions in training, education, organisation, and my last position was head of the unit for international arms cooperation. I was retired in end of September 1992 in the rank of lieutenant colonel, as I said already.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in 1993 you took up an assignment with the ECMM in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: That's correct. After my retirement, I was immediately contacted by the personnel officer of the Ministry of Defence with the question whether I would be prepared to join the ECMM as a short-term observer in the former Yugoslavia. As I agreed to that, I was given a six-month contract as a monitor to this organisation, starting in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us when the assignment came to an end.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The assignment ended legally in August 1993, but as I had some leave time left, I actually left the mission I think on the 26th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber give us a brief account or description of the role of the ECMM in Bosnia during your tenure, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The original mission of the ECMM was the supervision of the protection of the former Yugoslavia army from the newly independent states, mainly from Croatia and Bosnia. But later on this role was extended due to the situation as it developed, the crisis between the three parties, I would tell them, between the Bosniak side, the Croat side, and the Serbians. And this became, at least in 1993 and 1994, the main task of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you give us the geographic location of your AOR, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I was assigned to the regional centre Bosnia based in Zenica, covering legally the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we had no access at that time to the parts which were held by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And where were your headquarters located?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The headquarters was located at the Hotel Internacional in Zenica, Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The first day of your assignment would have been approximately early March 1993. Could you please describe for us how your day began, from the beginning of your tenure.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, I think my first day of duty was -- in the mission in Zenica was the 7th of March, I think. My first assignment was to act as an operations officer in the headquarters of the regional centre in Zenica. This had only a very short duration. Then I was reassigned to become a member to have Busovaca Joint Commission, a body which was just recently set up as a forum to mediate between the HVO and the Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you please state for the Trial Chamber the composition of the commission and the role of the commission, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The composition of the commission was that it had three parties: The ECMM, which also held the chair of the commission; and the members of the commission were also the deputy commander of the HVO forces in the area, which was based in Vitez; and the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the Armija BiH, based in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to recall for us the names of the commanders who served with you on the commission?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: On the commission, it was Colonel -- the name slipped out -- from the HVO, Tahic or something like that. I don't remember it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. And for the other side?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: For the other side, it was Colonel -- General Merdan, Dzemal Merdan. And I have to also add that both of them had one or two liaison officers also always with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, how often did you hold meetings? How often did the commission hold meetings?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: We met every morning, except on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And basically, what would be the agenda of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The typical agenda of the meeting would be first to hear the complaints from both sides, mainly concerning things that happened within the last night or during the last night or within the last 24 hours, and then to try to clarify the incidents of these events, find out whether they really happened or were just invented; and if they actually happened, we normally would decide to go to the spot and have a direct vision or a direct view of the facts that have to be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as a result of the meetings, did you do any reports on the said meetings?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Of course. Every member of the ECMM was obliged to write a daily report, which was then sent up the chain of command - that means the team reported to the coordination centre; we had at that time three in Bosnia, one based in Zenica as such, one based in Mostar or close to Mostar, and one based in Tuzla. These three coordination centres compiled the team reports into a daily report, which was then sent to the regional centre in Zenica, and these three incoming CC reports were then compiled to a singular regional centre report, which was presented to the headquarters in Zagreb before -- yeah, before midnight the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, could you tell us the structure of the reports. How did you write the report?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The reports were structured following a structure of the subordinate commands. That means it had an entry for each of the coordination centres. And they had a general statement about what happened in the general area. That means this statement was normally given to the operations officer by the head of the centre, stating -- giving his judgement of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if you were to be shown one of these reports, would you be able to recognise them, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I think I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's permission, may the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P264, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, having looked at the report, could you tell us what you recognise of the report and what you have to say on the report.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I recognise this as the daily report of the 8th of May, 1993 written by myself, and submitted to the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And it shows what transpired during the alleged meeting and the conclusions as to ...?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, perhaps, Colonel, we could go into individual situations. And we would be around mid-April now. And I'd like you to discuss with us a meeting that took place on the 14th of April. Could you tell us what transpired, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: On the 14th of April? In the morning meeting of the Busovaca Joint Commission, the HVO claimed that four HVO officers returning from the front line near Travnik had been kidnapped and witnesses on the scene described the vehicle which took the hostages away as a green truck. This green truck came to be more later on a synonym for a heavy equipment of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What action, if any, was taken as a result of the meeting and the information that you gleaned from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: We tried to find out whether this action really happened, and it was confirmed. But we could not find out the same day what happened to the kidnapped four officers, until very, very close to the exchange of the hostages. Later we were unable to locate them and to give any estimation of who actually held them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you make any reports to the representative of the 7th Muslim Brigade with respect to the allegations that were made in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: We didn't -- as far as I know, we didn't make a report to the commander of the 7th Brigade, but we made -- brought the claim to the attention of the 3rd Corps Armija BiH representative in the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On the next day, it would have been the 15th of April, 1973, and did you learn anything -- 1993 -- and did you learn anything further with respect to the kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Not with respect to the kidnapping, but at that day, as far as I recall, another kidnapping happened directly in Zenica, where the commander of one of the two HVO brigades which were based in Zenica was kidnapped on his way to his office in the morning. His, I think, four bodyguards were shot dead, as well as one civilian victim who happened to be in the vicinity of the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber state for us the name of the alleged kidnapped commander.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: His name was Colonel Totic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And by the 16th of April, could you tell us if the commission still existed, and if not, why.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, the Busovaca Joint Commission never met again after the 14th of April, due to the events that started with the kidnapping mainly of Colonel Totic. The joint commission was never legally or formally dissolved, but none of the members involved, the sides, saw any benefit any more in any of the meetings. And I have to add also that on the -- I think on the 16th as well, the two HVO brigades based in Zenica were disarmed by Armija BiH and dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How would you describe the situation in the area now?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The tension was very high after these events, and resulted finally in a restart of fighting mainly in the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, there came a time after that when you proceeded to -- on leave. Could you tell us when you left and for how long.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, I left on the 19th on a planned leave. The way I got out was using a convoy which was evacuating mainly personnel of international organisations who felt that the threat was too high now, and my task was to escort this convoy from Zenica to Split. And from Split I went on leave. I came back, as far as I recall, on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you got back to the 30th of April, could you tell us where you were now seconded to.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: After my return from leave, I was, as the commission was dissolved, again appointed as operations officer in the HQ RC in Zenica, took over this position immediately. And a few days later, as far as I recall, I had also to take over the task of a Greek monitor who was leaving for Sofia, I think, who had up to that time served as a connection to a group of, as they called them, Arabs, or Mujahedin, in negotiating a possible exchange of hostages between the Bosniak and the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: These negotiations, Colonel, were they to have taken up the time up to the end of your tenure? Did it?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Almost, yes. It took me busy for -- until the exchange actually happened, which was, according to my memory, the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, could you in chronological order tell us exactly what took place with respect to the exchange and how you eventually got these prisoners of war exchanged. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, actually, the negotiations started when I was on leave and were on the ECMM side done by Mr. Dagos, the Greek monitor. He briefly -- but sufficiently, of course -- briefed me on the events that happened during my absence before he left, because I had to take over. These negotiations were kept on a very, very low profile, even in the ECMM mission in Zenica only the head of the office and the chief interpreter knew about it. And I had to continue to keep this on low key in order not to involve too many people in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With whom did you -- who were the parties? Who were the negotiating parties? And who represented who?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The parties were an unknown person representing, as we said, the Arab Group, myself, and I had to convey the request from the Arab Group to HVO and to Armija BiH through two contact persons, both of them being the chief of the military police from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And this unknown person, could you -- would you be able to describe for us what he looked like and his ethnic background for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, according to his appearance, I would say he was from Northern Africa, maybe Tunisia. He was in his mid-30s, I would say, slim, about -- almost 180 high; very well educated in his behaviour, very polite. But he never disclosed his name and he never -- I never had a chance to address him by his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In Bosnia, how would such a person be referred to as?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, the group he was representing, actually would have been called the Mujahedin in normal phrases.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. After days of negotiations, there finally came a time when the actual handing over took place, or the actual exchange took place. Could you tell us what transpired in this said day. And I believe it would have been the 17th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I think I have to start with the 14th, when actually the request was made that HVO should set a date for the exchange. And the HVO on my -- after my transmittal of the request proposed the 17th at 12.00 as the date for the exchange to be. This date was accepted by the Arabian Group and they additionally requested that the exchange should take place on three locations -- at three locations at the same time. The three locations they gave was, number one, in Travnik in front of the PTT building. The PTT building at that time was the place where a joint headquarters between HVO and the Armija BiH had been set up. One could look at this joint headquarters as a follow-up of the Busovaca Joint Commission, except that ECMM was not represented in this body, but we used it as a platform for negotiations and mediation. The second place was the Mediapan factory, a wood factory close to the Kaonik prison. And the third place was in front of the Hotel Internacional in Zenica, the headquarters of the ECMM, of course. It was requested that at all three locations representatives from all four sides which were involved - the four -- I'm now talking about four sides being ECMM as a mediator, the Arab Group as the requestor, I would like to say; the HVO as holding one part of the hostages; and the Armija BiH as holding the other part of the hostages. And it was also requested that three means of communications, independently, had to be set up between the three locations, so we used the normal PTT telephone line as one means, and two other means were provided by the British Battalion based in Vitez. One was a radio link and one of a satellite telephone link.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you say, then, the exchange went through smoothly?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Sorry, I cannot say this, because we encountered a number of problems during the preparation -- during the actual exchange. As I said, the exchange was planned for 12.00. Everything was prepared to that, and then we had problems in communication, language-wise, because one of the representatives of the Arab Group - and this was the one that was with me in the Mediapan factory - didn't speak any English and didn't speak any Serbo-Croat or whatever, so it was very difficult to make him understand at what stage the preparations had reached and what he could communicate to his counterparts on the other side. This resulted in a delay of more than four and a half hours, so actually we could start with the exchange of the hostages by about 4.30 and we were through about -- after 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you have to take your convoy to any particular place to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes. The arrangement was like this: That in the factory -- the wood factory close to Kaonik the, I think, 12 Muslim hostages should be taken by myself and then transported to Zenica in front of the Hotel Internacional, where they should be exchanged against the Colonel Totic and two other Croat people that had been kidnapped in the meantime from a radio station in Zenica. One was I think a journalist and the other one was a radio operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Anything unusual at the Hotel Internacional in Zenica when you went to complete the exchange?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes. The unusual thing was that the police officers, which were normally based in front of the hotel for our protection, were not on the spot and no local police or other military personnel could be seen. But a big number of soldiers, most of them wearing masks but none of them wearing any military insignia, were around the place, in front of the hotel, on the roof of the football stadium, which is quite -- just opposite the hotel, and in the vicinity. They were heavily armed not only with their normal small arms but also with RPGs, which means anti-tank rocket missile, and also four battle I think 20-millimetre gun mounted on a 5-tonne truck. And this gun had been seen before by us and was a part of the equipment of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In your opinion, then, which unit would you say that all these soldiers came from?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I assumed that all of them were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were tasked to assure the exchange on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And finally, was the exchange completed?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The exchange was completed. The Muslim hostages were released from the British armoured personnel carriers and taken over by the Muslim side or Arab side, I would say, and put into, I think, two trucks and transported away, and at the same time Colonel Totic was released from a small vehicle and handed over to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you eventually have what one would say a final meeting with respect to this exchange, and with whom did you have it?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I had a visit the next day, the following day, by our -- by my negotiating partner from the Arab side, who thanked me for the successful exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, during your tenure in Bosnia from April until July 1993, did you have cause to meet with Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, I had. Although the -- normally the contacts with General Hadzihasanovic were done by Mr. Thebault, our head of the regional office himself, on three or four occasions, he asked me to accompany him on these occasions, more or less to be a witness for the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us or give us your opinions with respect to this gentleman, Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic, to me, occurred as a real military leader, who had a certain, I would say -- I'm missing the correct English word for it -- who impressed -- could impress people positively. And I think due to his background he was a real military leader on top of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you say that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was somebody who was definitely in charge? Would you say that? Did you get that impression?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: He was definitely in charge of all troops of the 3rd Corps Armija BiH. But I could not confirm that he was in charge or on top of the groups of Mujahedin that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: To whom did you make your complaints with respect to the Muslim units in the area? To whom did you lodge your complaints?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: These complaints normally were lodged by Mr. Thebault to General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us what usually was the response.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The response normally was, if it was concerning the 7th Muslim Brigade, that he would take care of the case. As far as it concerned the Mujahedin, the answer normally was "These are not under my control."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And during your tenure there, did you see any progress with respect to the complaints that you made? Did you see any progress?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes. At least, as far as the 7th Muslim Brigade is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I believe that you would have had contact with Mr. Merdan. Could you give us a brief synopsis of what -- how this gentleman reached out to you, what are your impressions of him, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I had been working with Mr. Merdan in the joint commission for about six weeks on a daily basis, so I think I got to know him very well, and he impressed me as a person, a person who was very reasonable, clear-thinking, and straightforward. According to his background, being a naval officer, he was not in the position, according to my judgement, to be the deputy commander of an army corps. For instance, when we were on the ground and I found infantry positions in a very inappropriate place, where I would have normally asked people to move to a suitable place he never made such an attempt, because obviously this was not of his concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about your concerns and your complaints with respect to problems or reports that you may have received? Would you say that they were well received by Mr. Merdan and were they acted upon?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Mr. Merdan took all of our complaints very seriously. In many cases it turned out that he was poorly briefed before he came to the meeting by his headquarters, and in many cases he had to ask for a time-out in order to contact General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So Mr. Merdan would have referred the complaints up to Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your final day in office and as a consequence the end of your tenure was sometime around the end of May 1993; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: The end of May was the end of my term in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In that AOR.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: In that -- well, actually, in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: At that time, I went on leave again, until, I think, end of May, and after my return, I was reassigned to be the head of the coordination centre in Tuzla, in Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before your -- before proceeding on leave, you would have written a final report as to what transpired during the tenure; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I wrote a final report on the hostage exchange I think the day after the exchange happened; this would be the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if you were to see that report again, would you be able to recognise the same?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: For sure, because I keep a copy in my personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P155, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I recognise this as my final report written after the hostage exchange. And I have to correct my previous statement. It was not the 18th but the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, on the last page -- the pages are not numbered, but on the very last page, 00707018. Would that be a list of the hostages that were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Correct. This was a list of the hostages exchanged. Under A, these are the names of the hostages that were handed over from HVO to Armija BiH. Under B and C are those -- the Croat names of the persons that had been handed over to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, and finally, your presence in Bosnia as a negotiator with the ECMM, did you see it having any effect in any way on what transpired?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, looking back to the time, I have to say that for sure the presence of the ECMM monitors in Bosnia had a positive effect insofar that the situation would have probably been much worse and even fighting much tougher without their presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. Benjamin. I'm giving the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Schellschmidt. I would like to thank you for having given us the opportunity to meet you during our preparations. For the record, I'm going to introduce myself to you again. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. As the President has already explained to you, I would like to ask you certain questions that arise from the questions of my learned friend, but I'm also going to put to you some general questions in order to set the context when you were on your tour of duty in Bosnia. You arrived in Zenica on 7 March 1993 as a member of the European Monitoring Mission, and after a certain while spent in the regional centre in Zenica, you were deployed to the Busovaca Commission. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, the chief of the regional centre of the monitoring mission of the European Union was a French diplomat whose name was Jean-Pierre Thebault; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were aware of the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised as an independent state, that it had been admitted as a member of the United Nations, and that immediately after that it had been attacked and that most of the country had been occupied by the Army of Republika Srpska. Were you aware of all of these facts?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, I was briefed on these facts on the -- in the start of my mission at the headquarters of the ECMM in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not have any precise information about the relationship between the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and the Croatian Defence Council; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I had been briefed on the problems between these two factions as well during my introductory tour in Zagreb, so I had a certain amount of knowledge about the problems between these two parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You obtained additional information when you arrived in Zenica, and when you were told that between the HVO and the BH army there was quite a lot of tension and even fighting in Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and in Busovaca. Did you obtain such information?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, in order to find a solution to matters that were in dispute, a cessation of hostilities was established and attempts were made to prevent new fighting from breaking out and a commission was established in Busovaca which was called the Busovaca Commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Busovaca Commission, and in response to a question from my learned colleague you told us about the composition of this composition [as interpreted] - meetings were held in this commission on a daily basis either in Busovaca or in Vitez. These towns at the time were under HVO control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For these reasons, as Armija members were not able to pass through territory under HVO control, the European monitors and you yourself drove the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, Dzemal Merdan, from Zenica on a daily basis and other officers as well. You drove them to a meeting held in the headquarters of the European monitors in Busovaca or Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to discussions about the problems that the parties -- both parties presented to the commission, you wanted to take immediate and direct action in the field, and quite often many members of the commission or some of the members went into the field in order to observe the situation directly and in order to attempt to resolve any problems. Is this the method that you used?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, this was a method which we used. And in the beginning, this seemed to be a very effective method in order to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went into the field with Armija and HVO representatives, as an experienced soldier you were in a position to observe that the BH Armija was in the process of being established and that in many situations it was a matter of groups that had organised themselves and the local commanders were those who were in fact in charge. Is this something that you were able to observe? Was this a conclusion you could draw?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, my observation at that time was that there was no real military structure established at that time, and those who called themselves being a company or being a battalion normally were more or less smaller groups of men who had picked up weapons and appointed one of them, mainly -- and sometimes, in some cases, the mayor or in some cases another leading person in the village, to be their commander. So I would say that the military chain of command at that time did not really exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you were able to observe a significant difference between the members of the 3rd Corps Command and you described Commander Hadzihasanovic and his deputy, Merdan, you described them as professional soldiers and you said that they were trying to establish the Armija. So you were able to observe differences between them and the soldiers in the field who were not professional soldiers but were organised in the way that you have just described. Were you able to notice such a difference, a difference which also concerned the way in which military discipline was regarded?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, this is more or less true. There was a great difference between the officers in the headquarters of the Armija of the 3rd Corps, which in most cases had some military background, and the forces in the field, where the military background mainly was the experience from their military service as conscripts in previous years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also able to notice that quite frequently the deputy commander Dzemal Merdan wasn't in a position to issue orders to the local commanders. He more frequently used discussion and negotiations in order to ensure that they understood that the order was justified and that it was necessary to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This is correct, and I would like to refer to my previous statement about the character of Dzemal Merdan as it appeared to me, not being a person depending on giving orders, rather than on persuading people to do certain things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, would it be correct for me to say that when I previously spoke to you you described the situation by saying that sometimes you had the impression that Armija commanders, 3rd Corps commanders, in fact also used the Busovaca Commission in order to discipline and organise their very own army? Is that the impression that you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This is a very good description of the impressions I had sometimes, that we have been used - by we, I mean the commission - have been used to as a chain of communications to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this explanation of yours, you also said that it was very difficult to establish a corps. And if I am interpreting what you said correctly, you said that in order to create a corps, if you're starting from scratch, you need up to seven years; and if there are brigades that already exist, in such a case this would require three years. I then asked what sort of position Enver Hadzihasanovic was in. Could you please tell me whether you remember what your answer to my question was on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I think I quoted an American saying, being a "Mission: Impossible."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what you told me. Nevertheless, in spite of the situation that the 3rd Corps was in, could you confirm, Mr. Schellschmidt, that the Armija command and the BH army strove to cooperate with the European Community and the European monitors? It was open to suggestions and carried out the decisions that had been reached at the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, of course the Armija BiH was always open for suggestions. I'm not so sure about -- that they were really successful in implementing the decision of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you about your involvement in the exchange of these foreign combatants. I would now like to go back to the previous period, the early period when you worked in the Busovaca Commission. Would it be correct to say that information about certain foreigners being arrested by the HVO was information that you received a lot earlier? You received it in March from the Red Cross. You examined this information at a meeting of the Busovaca Commission, and on that occasion Dzemal Merdan informed you that certain international Islamic non-governmental organisations were also requesting that these individuals be released, and as a result you decided to deal with this issue, to examine the issue at one of the commission's meetings. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, this is correct. We learned about the fact that some individuals had been detained by HVO earlier in one of the missions, and in the course of the UN's. I together with another ECMM monitor visited the military prison in Kaonik and had a chance to talk to four people of mainly Arabian background which were detained there. Two of them -- one of them was obviously a journalist, having a Turkish accreditation; another one claimed to be an aid worker for a Saudi Arabian organisation; the other two also claimed to be aid workers, but could not give us any -- the name of any organisation they had been affiliated to. Actually, I understand that this was the very first time that this prison has been visited by any international organisations; even the International Red Cross didn't have access to this prison before. But at that time, there was not any connection or vision of any hostage exchange. It was just dealing with detained Arabian peoples, and the -- we made an attempt to get them free. HVO agreed under the condition that these four people -- I think they were still talking about four people -- would be taken immediately to Croatia and sent back to their home countries in order to prevent them staying into -- on Bosnian territory. The problem for us was to arrange transport into Croatia and our headquarters in Zagreb did not respond in any way to our request for authorisation to do so, and the Red Cross, of course, due to their mandate was not able to do it as well. So this was not accomplished, and in the meantime the exchange question came out and these four people were among those being exchanged on 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have a few more questions that concern the information you first received about foreigners in Kaonik. Their presence was denied and it was then accepted by Colonel Blaskic, who made it possible for you to make the visit you have mentioned. But you also found out that there were other Arabs who were detained elsewhere and they had been arrested when arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: It's correct that at first the presence of the four in Kaonik was denied and later on accepted by Colonel Blaskic. We also were told about other Arabs being detained, mainly on their way between the Croatian border and Central Bosnia, but we had no certain information where they were held prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking to the commander of the prison in Kaonik, Mr. Aleksovski, you found out that they had quite a lot of money on them, over one million dollars in marks, German marks. And from Colonel Blaskic you also found out that they had weapons and this is the reason for which they were imprisoned. Is this the information that you obtained at the time?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, we were told that they carried -- or at least one of them carried a big amount of money in US dollars and in German marks. Allegedly all of them were carrying hand weapons, and one -- on one person a mini camera was also found, which was deemed to be inappropriate for aid workers. And this was given as the main reason for their detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people that you spoke to said that they had permission to enter the country and all that they requested that you do was that you should inform the Islamic centre in Zenica about the fact that they had been detained. Is that all that these individuals asked you to do on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, of course they asked us to assist them to get freed and it's true that they asked us to inform the Islamic centre in Zenica, which of course happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was quite clear to you that those individuals were not members of the BH army at the time that you visited them.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This is true. We never considered them to be members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, let's now move on to the subject of the information that you had about the kidnapping of four HVO soldiers and the kidnapping of Mr. Totic in Zenica. My learned colleague has asked you detailed questions about this. Would it be correct to say that following the protest that was lodged with you the HVO blocked all the roads around Zenica and they threatened to divide Zenica into a part under Croatian control and into another part under the control of the Armija?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- actually not aware of such a threat. It's actually the first time I hear today. But it's true - talking about the dividing Zenica - but it's true that, I know about the threat to cut all road connections into Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Greek monitor, Dagos, was responsible to follow the -- this issue, the issue of the individuals who were kidnapped, and he was fully involved in this matter; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. He followed the whole matter from the ECMM side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since at the very beginning the HVO lodged a protest with your commission and they said that they suspected that the 7th Muslim Brigade was involved in the kidnapping, the 3rd Corps of the BH army and all its units, in an attempt to show that the Armija had nothing to do with the kidnapping, immediately made it possible for the European monitors to visit all the places in which it was suspected that these kidnapped men might be present. So HVO members went to these places together with the European monitors.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Well, actually, these things happened during my absence from Zenica, but I can confirm that members of our mission had access to these places and they checked them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, that was my next question: From the 19th to the 30th of April, you were on leave. And with regard to the events that took place during that period, the only information you had about these events is information that your colleague, Mr. Dagos, provided you with when he was leaving the mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned from leave you no longer worked with a team or in the commission. You assumed the duties of an operations officer in the regional centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your task was to collect daily reports drafted by team members in the field. You had to put all these reports together and then send these reports to the relevant institutions in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, with one small addition: The teams reported to their respective coordination centre, which normally controlled two to three teams. These coordination centres - we had three of them - compiled a report from these three team reports and transmitted it to the regional centre in Zenica, where I had to compile these CC reports into one report for the headquarters, which also had to include the judgement and the statements from the head of the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct if I said that while you were in the Busovaca Commission you compiled daily reports on the basis of the information you had yourself; and when you worked in the regional centre you weren't an immediate witness of events, you had to rely on the reports that were drafted by your colleagues? Would my assessment be correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, this assessment is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's perhaps time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for having pointed out that it's time for our break. It is now quarter to 4.00. We will resume at 4.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor to resume your cross-examination, Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, is it correct that the role of a negotiator on behalf of the European monitors that you had, that you took it over from Mr. Dagos on the 11th May 1993?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From that then day onwards you were a witness to everything that was taking place during the negotiations. Before that time, all you had was information from Mr. Dagos or the information that you read subsequently in daily reports. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: It's correct insofar as I got my information from Dagos. There was almost nothing about this negotiations for obvious reasons in the daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment you took over this negotiating mission, the ECMM was in contact with the representatives of these foreigners only via yourself and only after that the information that you had received you would send to the HVO, the BiH army, and the International Red Cross Committee; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: It's correct. The only person that was directly involved was myself and my interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to ask the usher to show to the witness eight photos. The originals are in colour. Therefore, I'm going to ask the witness to put them on the ELMO so we can all see them. And I have a set of photocopies for the Trial Chamber and my learned friends. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence came into possession of these photos from a potential Defence witness who due to certain reasons can no longer be called to testify. He was one of the monitors himself and he was on the spot during the events. I'm going to ask the witness, should he recognise these photos, to mark them and the Defence is going to tender these photos into evidence. The Trial Chamber is aware of the reasons for which the Defence is not going to be able to call this witness. The Defence has decided to use this witness as a military consultant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, could you please place these photos on the overhead projector. We would like to see the photos that you're looking at in colour. Could you please tell us whether you recognise these photos.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously this photograph shows the moment when the exchanged Arab hostages were put into these two vehicles and -- in order to carry them away. It was at the -- It was towards the end of the exchange procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To speed things along, I would like the witness to look at all the eight photographs, and I am going to ask him to sign the ones that he has recognised and put today's date, and when tendering these photos into evidence I would like to Trial Chamber to give them just one number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I proceed in this way, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the second photo on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any observations to this procedure? The Defence would like to show the witness all the eight photographs at a time. They would like the witness to put today's date and his name on the photographs that he recognises. The witness has already told us that he has recognised the first photo. Mrs. Benjamin or Mr. Mundis, do you have any objections to this fashion of procedure?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the format, we don't have any objections. It could go in as a bundle. But as to what is going to transpire when the witness identifies each one, then, only then can we say. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, do you recognise the following photo?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I recognise this as a photograph showing a view from Zenica. As I recall, from the roof or top of the Hotel Internacional to the river upwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at photo number 3.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph also shows the area in front of the Hotel Internacional, and then on the left-hand side you can see that -- a track-mounted four-barrelled gun with a number of people standing on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the next photo.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This again is a photo taken during the exchange, that means at the end of the exchange. On the left-hand side at the bottom is one to have British armoured personnel carriers. Behind that, a white car I cannot really recognise. I think it's one of the vehicles used to transport the hostages. And the white one, you have already seen on the first picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on to the next photo, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Okay. I recognise this photograph as well. It shows, again, in the foreground the two armoured personnel carriers, and myself in between them, the guy with the blue cap and the hand-held radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This again is a photograph of the same scene, obviously taken out of the upper floors from the hotel, and showing the background, the football stadium I was referring to earlier in my statement. And this moment, which is obviously close to the end of the procedure, the roof of the stadium is already emptied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the next photo, please. Can you look at it.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: I think this single person in front is my mediator from the Arab side, because he was always wearing a brown suit and a cap. And also -- I cannot recognise the face. I think it's him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last photo, please.

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: This again shows part of the exchange. The hostages are --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness was there, he has recognised himself in one of the photos, and he is well aware of the situation in all the other photos. Again I would like to ask the witness to mark every photo, put numbers from 1 to 8 on them, put today's date and sign them. And the Defence would like to tender these eight photos into evidence as a single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Sir, can you put your name, today's date, and sign every photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I with the Trial Chamber's indulgence, please, with respect to number 2, that's the only one that I think the Prosecution want to object on, on the grounds of relevance. I really do not see how it relates to the others and what we are in fact talking about. So that is the only objection that we would want to have, number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 2, which depicts a bridge and a river, what is the relevance of this photo? Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will -- can withdraw this photo, however we have received it from the witness who has taken all of these photos and he photographed the bridge and the river from the same place and -- showing the area in front to have Hotel Internacional. If the Trial Chamber would like us to withdraw this photo from the bundle, we are happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have this photo in colour? Because the only thing we have is a black-and-white copy. Do we have this photo in colour as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The witness has seen the photo in colour. I would respectfully suggest that he should sign it, because we would like to tender into evidence the colour photos. We have made black-and-white copies for the Trial Chamber to help it follow what the witness is explaining. If the Trial Chamber would like to see the colour photos before rendering their decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Chamber would like to see the colour photos. To avoid wasting any more time, I would like to ask just one question arising from photo number 2. Can you please put it on the ELMO. Witness, you are looking at photo number 1. We can see two vans and also persons who are masked, and in the back there is the public. Behind the van, there are bushes. Can you please look behind the bushes. In the photo we see two persons in military uniforms, and one of them is carrying a gun. According to you, who were these two persons in military uniforms? What do you think? Can you please look at the photo. Who are these two people? One of them is carrying a rifle. Could you tell us about these two people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think both of them were part of the military group that surrounded the area, as I described earlier. Most of them were wearing masks; some of them did not, and I assume that these two belong to that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the two persons belonged to the group; is that the conclusion that you draw based on this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the only question I had. Can you please put your name and today's date on the photo, on the photos. We are returning to the Defence the photo of the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher is going to show these photos which have been signed by the witness to the Prosecution, to the Defence teams, and to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] Mr. President, I numbered and marked seven pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are returning the eighth one to the Defence, because they have withdrawn it from the bundle and they are not tendering the eighth photo into evidence. Mr. Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for these photos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH182.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, you were talking about the teams and the members of the Busovaca Commission and how they used to write daily reports to be delivered to coordination centres. The coordination centres would deliver them to the regional centre and then the operations officer in the regional centre would draft a report that would be sent to Zagreb. Is it correct, Mr. Schellschmidt, that during a certain period of time when the European Monitoring Mission, on the basis of their daily observations and conversations that they had as well as on the reports that they received from the field, could provide a certain opinion on the most significant problems; and when that happened a special report would be drafted on the political and military situation and this report would be drafted by the head of mission and would deliver it to your superior command in Zagreb? Was that the procedure? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, this was in general the case and the procedure. Special reports could be written by a single monitor who had been tasked with the specific task, or by the head of the regional centre, either on request from the headquarters or on a decision of the person concerned. There were no set dates and events on which special reports had to be written. It was up to the discretion of the one submitting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, going to--

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to ask for the witness to be shown a special report dated the 1st of May. This report was drafted by the head of mission in Zenica, Mr. Jean-Pierre Thebault. We have a sufficient number of copies for everybody. Mr. President, this document was provided to the Defence from the Blaskic case. There's also a French translation of the document and an identical document was disclosed to us by the Prosecution in agreement with the European Union, when they received the European Union's approval for these documents to be disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, do you recognise this report as one of the special reports that the head of mission drafted on certain military, political, and other issues relevant to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this as one of the special reports -- although I have not seen this specific one before, because as you see it's absolutely confidential. That means that the head of the regional centre had not circulated it inside our organisation. But it is one of those special reports written on specific occasions, and this one at the end, I understand, contains very specific recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since this is a recognisable document, i.e., a special report by the European monitors, and the witness is aware of the procedure, and since this is an official document of the European Monitoring Mission, I would like to tender this document into evidence as a very relevant Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, the Defence would like to tender into evidence the report that the witness does not know. He has explained to us that this report is a confidential report and that's why he was not aware of its contents. However, what is in the report he doesn't contest. What is your position on this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's precisely the reason why we would want to object. This witness is not the author of that report. He says quite clearly that it was a confidential report. He knows nothing of what is inside this report. And my friend said she's submitting the report or putting it into evidence based on the relevance of the report. I can't understand. Relevance to what? Is it relevance to the evidence that's before us or -- because if the witness himself says quite clearly "I cannot say -- comment on it because it was confidential. I am not the author of the report," and all he could really agree on is the format of the report. So I would want to think that clearly this report should not be allowed to be entered into evidence, because it does not -- the foundation has not been properly laid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish to respond to the position put forth by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Some of the issues covered by this report have already been commented upon by the witness. I can continue and ask some additional questions, but I don't deem this to be necessary because so far our position has been that all the official reports drafted by the European monitors and the UNPROFOR that the Prosecution has tendered, we would accept as being authentic and we -- and these reports are admitted into evidence. This procedure was applied to the report dated July referring to the importance of the supply flows, and the witness who was testifying about the situation in Gornji Vakuf recognised that document although he hadn't seen it before. For this reason, since this is an official document, since the witness has already spoken about some of the issues covered by this report and since so far none of the sides to this procedure has had any objections to such documents being admitted into evidence, I believe there is ample reason for this exhibit to be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to deliberate, because this is a decision that has to be made jointly by the three Judges. After our deliberation, we are going to render a decision. But in order for the Judges to be absolutely clear, I would like to ask the Defence the following: On page 1 of the document on the right-hand side, I can see "Exhibit P386" or something like that. Does that mean that this is an exhibit that belongs to the Prosecution in another case?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a Prosecution exhibit in the Naletilic case. I believe that on the top you can see that. And the French translation, in the Blaskic case, the same document was used and it was translated into French, and that's why we are using this translation. This is an identical document, absolutely identical document as the document that we have received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. In the French version, there is a number, 00850587. Is that the Prosecution number?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is also the number given to this in the Blaskic case, and this is the number under which the Prosecution disclosed this document to the Defence team in this case. So this is a Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mrs. Benjamin, would you like to comment upon these clarifications by the Defence? The Defence has told us that this document comes from the Prosecution, that it was tendered into evidence in another case. What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's just the point. The Prosecution is not objecting on the grounds of authenticity. The objection is raised on the grounds of relevance to this particular case. That document has absolutely no relevance to this particular case. The objection is not against authenticity; it's against relevance, and it certainly does not apply to this case. In addition, the witness himself has said "I don't know what's in there. I am not the author, and I can't say;" you know, "except for format, I cannot say anything else about the document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The Judges are going to deliberate on this issue, and we shall inform you about our decision regarding the admission of this exhibit into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the document number P264.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schellschmidt, this document was drafted on the 8th of May, 1993. Can you please look at page 2. The document was signed by yourself. There is your initial and your family name, and then it says "/OPS." Does this mean that you drafted this document as the operations officer in the regional centre? Is this what the abbreviation stands for?

utterances.speaker: DIETER SCHELLSCHMIDT
utterances.text: It's correct. It's my name and my function.
